Issued at 143 PM CDT Thu Sep 17 2026

Today - Tonight: Mostly dry, Isolated Showers South of I-90

The wave and weak moisture transport responsible for this 
morning's rainfall have largely shifted eastward this afternoon 
and along with them, more widespread rainfall. However, can't 
rule out some lingering isolated showers south of I-90 through 
the afternoon as lingering low level moisture across the region 
along with some weak isentropic ascent on the 305K surface 
should be enough for said development. These forcings move east
overnight with cloudy conditions remaining as we head into 
Friday morning. 

Friday - Saturday: Widespread Rainfall and Flooding Potential

A 500hPa shortwave trough is expected to eject off of the 
closed low currently situated across the Pacific Northwest this 
afternoon, moving eastward tonight while an associated surface 
low moves into the Upper Midwest. The warm front associated with
the surface low moves into the Upper Mississippi River Valley 
Friday morning and stalls across the region which will be the 
catalyst for a widespread rainfall event across the Upper 
Mississippi River Valley Friday into Saturday. 

South of this boundary, a very moist airmass is expected to be 
in place, characterized by PWATs around 1.7-1.9 inches. 
Moisture transport associated with a strengthening 850hPa low 
level jet will also nudge into the boundary, ushering the 
saturated airmass northward which combined with strong 850hPa 
warm air advection and 800-700 frontogenesis should provide 
ample forcing for rainfall development. This rainfall could be 
fairly efficient at times Friday given the saturated atmosphere
though an overall lack of instability throughout the day should
hinder convectively enhanced rainfall. Heading into the 
overnight hours Friday, the aforementioned moisture transport 
strengthens further per the 17.15z RAP while MUCAPE increases to
around 250-500 J/kg at which time some convectively enhanced 
rainfall and rain rates of 1+ inches per hour would become more
favorable. Storm motion vectors also parallel the boundary 
during this time which leads to the potential for training 
showers/storms as we head into Saturday morning. Given the 
favorable set-up for widespread rainfall which could be heavy at
times, confidence is fairly high that amounts should be around 
1-3 inches (30-60%) though locally higher amounts of 4+ inches 
are possible, especially where convectively enhanced 
precipitation occurs. 

While confidence in efficient rainfall and a few inches of 
rainfall is fairly high, the location of said heaviest rainfall 
is less certain with a couple scenarios in place. The first and
higher confidence scenario (70-80%) is that the axis of 
heaviest rainfall develops generally along and south of I-90 
where the various CAMs, and by association the 17.12z HREF, are
currently in the best agreement as to where convectively 
enhanced rainfall is most likely to develop overnight Friday 
into Saturday. The second scenario brings the heaviest rainfall 
a bit further north and a bit further south with those along 
I-90 largely being spared the heaviest rainfall (20-30%). While 
confidence is higher in the first scenario, some of the CAM 
guidance does suggest higher rainfall rates are favored across 
northeast Iowa which may result in this axis tending towards the
second scenario. Overall, it appears to be more of a question 
of where will the axis of highest rainfall amounts occur rather 
than a question of if it will occur. 

From an impacts standpoint, areal flooding and river rises are 
likely for areas that receive the greatest rainfall amounts and
for those areas that received more abundant rainfall amounts 
earlier this week. Flash flooding is possible, although this 
threat appears to be greatest overnight Friday into Saturday 
when convectively enhanced rainfall and training storms are 
favored. For additional information, please see the Hydrology 
section. 

Sunday - Early Next Week: Additional Rainfall and Cooler

The upper wave responsible for the widespread rainfall moves 
east of the region Sunday while the aforementioned upper low 
begins to shift eastward across the northern United States. The 
quasi-stationary boundary responsible for the rainfall Friday-
Saturday is currently expected to remain stalled across 
northeast Iowa into southwest Wisconsin which should result in 
some additional showers and storms along the boundary as the 
upper low continues eastward. The upper level pattern remains 
fairly active through the beginning of the new week while the 
aforementioned boundary remains situated across northeast Iowa 
and southwest Wisconsin, resulting in additional chances for 
showers and storms (20-50%). 

Apart from the rainfall potential, cooler temperatures are on 
the horizon with highs topping out in the upper 50s to low 60s 
for the end of the weekend and into next week per the 17.13z
